activities.anchor: An AND gate is a few transistors wired so that its output wire sits high only when both input wires sit high
activities.caption: the algebra and its machine — drag the divider
activities.name: gateAlgebraCompare

config.prompt: Drag between the mathematics and its machine:

before.label: 1854 — the algebra
before.text: logic on paper: conjunction, disjunction, negation, with laws of their own

after.label: 1937 — the wiring
after.text: switching circuits embody the same algebra — logic gains a machine, engineering gains a mathematics

config.why: The 1937 master's thesis showed the wiring IS the algebra: a machine could compute anything expressible in logic — the digital age followed from that observation.

activities.anchor: The two-input tables are worth knowing cold.
activities.caption: pair each gate with its output signature
activities.name: gateTablesMatch

config.prompt: Pair each gate with its output signature:

pairs.right: 1 only on row 11 — both must agree
0 only on row 00 — inclusive: 1 even when both inputs are 1
0 only on row 11 — AND, then flipped
1 only on row 00 — OR, then flipped

config.why: Read each as a sentence: flip it; both must agree; one is enough; they must differ.

activities.anchor: and the alarm example shows why it matters
activities.caption: true or false — inclusive vs exclusive
activities.name: gateOrJudge

statements.s: A OR B is 0 when both inputs are 1.
statements.why: Exclusive-or's contract; the inclusive gate outputs 1 on every row except 00, including 11.

statements.s: The inclusive gate outputs 1 on every row except 00 — even the row where both inputs are 1.
statements.why: One yes is enough, and two yeses still count.

statements.s: XOR outputs 1 exactly when the inputs differ.
statements.why: The inequality detector: 1 on rows 01 and 10.

statements.s: A smoke-and-heat sensor pair must still trigger the bell when both fire at once.
statements.why: Inclusive wins here: both sensors firing is still a yes — mixing the two gates up is the most common contract error.

activities.anchor: they are how NAND and NOR can impersonate every other gate
activities.caption: find the faulty law
activities.name: gateLawsSpot

config.prompt: One entry in this laws list is wrong — click it:
lines: A·1 = A and A+0 = A — the laws that mirror ordinary arithmetic.
A·A = A and A+A = A — no powers or coefficients in logic.
A·Ā = 0 and A+Ā = 1 — a variable or its negation covers everything.
A + A·B = B — the bigger term always wins.
De Morgan: NOT(A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B).
config.correction: A + A·B = A (absorption): if A is true, the second term is irrelevant — verify it on a two-row table.
config.why: The laws diverge from ordinary algebra exactly where logic is stranger and better — absorption among them.

activities.caption: bet before you read on — the English trap
activities.name: gateNotRichPredict

config.q: In English, 'not rich and happy' means:
choices: At least one of rich, happy is absent — not both present
Both not rich and not happy
config.why: A = 1, B = 0 decides it: NOT(A AND B) is true while (NOT A) AND (NOT B) is false — 'not both' and 'both are not' are different claims.

activities.anchor: Every operator becomes a gate, every input a wire, nesting becomes depth.
activities.caption: the design loop, start to finish
activities.name: gateLoopOrder

config.prompt: Real design runs a loop — put it in order:
items: Write the truth table — the complete specification
Derive the expression from the rows that matter
Simplify with the laws — each component is money
Verify the table again — habit, not doubt
config.why: Expression to circuit and back: the loop is mechanical once the notation is yours.

activities.anchor: two half adders plus an OR — the detail is a standard exercise
activities.caption: call the chain length of a 32-bit adder
activities.name: gateRippleEst

config.prompt: A machine adds 32-bit integers by rippling carries — how many chained single-bit adder units does that take?
config.why: Chain n units, each carry feeding the next, and you get n-bit arithmetic: 32 for a 32-bit word, with the slowest signal traversing every stage; carry-lookahead logic computes carries in parallel to dodge the wait.
config.context: Deliberately simple, deliberately slow — the honest first draft.

activities.anchor: "3.2 GHz" means 3.2 billion synchronised ticks per second
activities.caption: does it remember? file each circuit
activities.name: gateMemorySort

config.prompt: Does it remember? Sort each circuit:

items.label: outputs depend only on present inputs
a circuit computing a sum digit
an output routed back into its own input
two gates wired to hold each other's state
devices that update only on the clock's edge
the XOR-and-AND pair of the half adder

config.why: Memory is feedback — a loop that holds its own state until actively changed; the metronome paces when it may change.
